newsitem.title: DENMARK: Interest in Danish 4 pct bond outweighs supply.
newsitem.headline: Interest in Danish 4 pct bond outweighs supply.

text.p: Interest in Danish four percent bonds is rising ahead of a possible June rise in the coupon floor but borrowers say they have no new issuance plans.

"We have noted increased investor interest in four percent bonds. Many see it as their last chance to get hold of the paper, therefore it is more attractive to issue four percent bonds now than previously," Peter Westphal, liquidity chief of Danish savings bank Spar Nord told Reuters on Thursday.
The Copenhagen Stock Exchange sets the minimum coupon rate twice-yearly, in June and December, according to an average of yields on specified fixed-interest, government and mortgage-backed bonds.
If current yields of an average 5.58 percent persist throughout the May 14 -June 13 review period the floor will be raised to five percent.

The exchange can also order an extraordinary adjustment if the averages alter significantly outside the review periods, as it did last October when it lowered the floor to four percent from six percent.

Approximately 30 billion crowns in commercial four percent paper has since been issued and a government four percent treasury note issued last January sold its full three-billion crown quota in minutes.
The low coupon offers tax advantages to some types of investors, mainly private buyers from Denmark and Germany.
Issuers say they have no plans to exploit the current surge in demand.

"We have a very favourable liquidity situation at the moment so we are not presently active in the loan market," said Kaj V. Holm, liquidity manager for the major borrowers Oeresundskonsortiet and Oeresundsforbindelse.
"We expect to return in the second half of 1997 and then we shall see if it is still possible to issue four percent bonds," he added.

Kommunekredit, a specialist lender to local authorities which has so far issued about three billion crowns in four percent paper, said it had no immediate plans for more and, contrary to Spar Nord, said it had observed no rise in demand.
"We are very client-driven and have not felt any pressure from our clients for this kind of loan so have have not given any consideration (to new issuance)," department head Jan Villadsen said.
"That doesn't mean that the possiblity is ruled out, just that it is not something actively on our agenda," he said.
